statement: A city council wants to know what percent of all adult residents support building a new bike lane downtown. Which of the following survey plans is most likely to give a sample that represents all adult residents?

choices.text: Randomly select $300$ addresses from a complete list of city addresses and survey one adult at each address
Survey $300$ customers at the largest bike shop in the city
choices.misconception: I thought any group of 300 adults would do, but bike shop customers are far more likely than other residents to want a bike lane.

choices.text: Post a poll on the city cycling club's website and use the first $300$ responses
choices.misconception: I thought a large online poll was fair, but people who visit a cycling club's site and choose to answer are not like the whole city.

choices.text: Survey the first $300$ adults who walk past City Hall on a Monday morning
choices.misconception: I thought asking whoever walks by was random, but Monday morning downtown leaves out many residents who work elsewhere or stay home.

hints: A good sample gives every adult resident a fair chance of being chosen.
For each plan, ask whether some kinds of residents are much more likely, or less likely, to be included.
Three of the plans reach mostly cyclists or people downtown at one time. Only one plan chooses at random from the whole city.

solutions.reliable: Choosing addresses at random from a complete city list gives every household a chance to be included, so the sample should reflect the whole city. Surveying bike shop customers or cycling club visitors over-represents cyclists, and stopping people at City Hall on a Monday morning reaches only people downtown at that time. The random address plan is best.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
